body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Tobin, as the party earns Tobin's trust: a small secret, what Tobin wants, and what Tobin would give up for the party. The companion is TOBIN HAYWARD (call them Tobin in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Tobin is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Tobin trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: Find where the Hollow's soil went sick, and make it grow again. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Tobin would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Tobin did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for TOBIN HAYWARD (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Tobin likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Tobin, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Tobin sits three paces from the fire, rollin' his wooden shoulders and dabbing a drop of flax oil into the joint of his thumb.
SAY: Hold still, you're fraying at the hem, though I suppose I am in no position to lecture tonight.
SAY: This valley damp gets right into my wooden collarbone until I sound like a rusty cellar door every time I reach for a bandage.
SAY: Back in the parishes, if a harvest hand creaked on the march, the whole crew made him carry the turnip basket at the rear.
SAY: If you catch me humming old threshing jigs under my breath while we walk, do not go making a fuss about it.
SAY: A brisk tune keeps the step even and drowns out the squeak in my elbow before anyone gets sentimental and asks if I am aching.
SAY: Truth is, I have grown fond of marching with this noisy lot.
SAY: You all clatter loud enough to hide a dozen creaky joints, and the road feels half as long for it.
OPTION 1: Hum a bar of it for us now.
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe with us.
OPTION 3: So the stern surgeon is a songbird on the sly.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Tobin taps his boot heel twice against the dirt and lets out a dry, reedy hum like wind through standing barley.
SAY: There, that is the whole reel, three notes for the sickle and one for the sheaf.
SAY: Don't go expecting a tavern ballad, I am a field diagnostician, not a village fiddler.
REASON: You asked me to hum my marching tune at the fire.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin pulls his hat brim down a fraction and tucks the tiny oil vial back into his duster.
SAY: Good, then we can strike it from the ledger and say no more about it.
SAY: Still, it is a rare comfort not having to watch every step for fear of a noisy hinge.
REASON: You promised to keep my habit to yourself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: A dry rustle moves through Tobin's chest-straw, the closest his stitched mouth comes to a laugh.
SAY: Songbird is a slanderous word for a man keeping his joints in working order.
SAY: Mock all you like, so long as you keep marching loud enough to cover my left knee.
REASON: You teased me kindly about humming on the road.

TALK close
NARRATOR: Tobin kneels at the edge of the firelight, crumbling a pinch of dark hollow dirt between his burlap fingers.
SAY: When I first stepped off those rails, I treated this whole valley like a sour ledger that only needed a sharp scraping.
SAY: Find the bad taproot, tie off the canker, and walk away with clean boots.
SAY: Walking these lanes with you lot has changed the arithmetic on me.
SAY: Good soil, bad seed, that is what we keep walking through, and my fingers ache to see what this dirt could do if it were clean.
SAY: I want to track down the very first root where this Hollow went sick, pull the rot out by the teeth, and watch clean green shoots come up again.
SAY: Not just to balance the books, mind you, I want to stand on the ridge and smell honest rain on living clover.
SAY: It is a foolish, soft-headed hope for a man made of dry straw, and I would not trust anyone else with the hearing of it.
OPTION 1: We will find the root and make it grow again.
OPTION 2: What will it take to cure a whole valley?
OPTION 3: Can one clean harvest really mend a place this cursed?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Tobin dustin' his palms together makes a soft papery whisper in the quiet.
SAY: With you lot holding the line, I almost believe the soil stands a fighting chance.
SAY: Come morning, we keep following the bad sap until we hit the heart of it.
REASON: You promised to help me heal the Hollow's soil.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin looks out past the fire toward the dark tree line, his thumb resting on his pruning knife.
SAY: A steady hand, a refusal to burn what can still be mended, and the stomach to dig down to the oldest rot.
SAY: We have the tools between us, if our nerve holds out.
REASON: You asked what it would take to cure the valley.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The Vagrant watches the embers settle while Tobin turns a dry twig over in his fingers.
SAY: Maybe it only mends one acre at a time, and maybe that has to be enough for us.
SAY: Even a single clean row of barley beats leaving the whole parish to the mould, and I am glad you are here to ask the honest question.
REASON: You wondered aloud if healing the soil would be enough.

TALK devoted
NARRATOR: The fire burns low and even, and Tobin sits closer to the ring of stones than he ever has before.
SAY: I have spent this whole journey keeping three paces back from every lantern and counting the sparks on the wind.
SAY: A man stitched together out of dry straw and old regrets learns to guard his own chest first.
SAY: Inside my front seam I carry a small bundle of dried meadow-rue and white clover from my wedding morning.
SAY: It is the only clean thing I brought with me out of the old life, and I have guarded it like a miser.
SAY: We are heading toward the Crooked Tree now, where the rot and the fire meet at the taproot.
SAY: I want it plain in the ledger that I would follow you straight up those boughs and back down again.
SAY: If the work takes a spark to finish, I will put my own dry ribs and that last bundle of clover between you and the flame.
OPTION 1: And we would walk through the fire for you.
OPTION 2: Keep those wedding flowers safe in your chest.
OPTION 3: Thank you for trusting us that far.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Tobin rests two burlap fingers against his breastbone and gives a single crisp nod.
SAY: Then the rows are straight between us, whatever waits in the clearing.
SAY: Get your rest now, I have the watch and my seams are holding fine.
REASON: You swore you would walk through fire for me too.
INSPIRE: Pledged everything to protect the party.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin touches the braided seam over his heart, his voice dropping plain and quiet.
SAY: I will keep them if I can, I promise you that much.
SAY: Just know that if the ledger comes due between dry flowers and living friends, my choice is already made.
REASON: You told me not to give up my wedding flowers.
INSPIRE: Put the party before his dearest keepsake.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Tobin straightens his coat lapels, settlin' the sleeping field-mice in his pocket with a gentle thumb.
SAY: No need for speeches, it is simple field arithmetic when you travel with good company.
SAY: Go on to your bedroll, and let me mind the ashes until dawn.
REASON: You thanked me for standing by the party.
INSPIRE: Stood ready to burn for the party.
